The cell options from the R examples, on matplotlib figures, and svg output.
lightbox is off, so only cells marked for panzoom open in it. Clicking any other
figure does nothing, unless [its cell](#c9) turns lightbox on with
`#| lightbox: true`.

```yaml
filters:
  - panzoom
```

Jupyter leaves the `panzoom` and `lightbox` options out of the code shown on the
page, unlike knitr. The **Code** button at the top shows the full source.

The plots share this setup and helper:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)


def walk(ax, n=200, title=None):
    ax.plot(np.cumsum(rng.normal(size=n)))
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
```

## panzoom on a cell {#c1 expect-open="panzoom" expect-hint="shown"}

A cell with `#| panzoom: true`. It opens in panzoom, with the hint line.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave"
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave."

x = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 400)
plt.plot(x, np.sin(x))
plt.show()
```

## Cell options {#c2 expect-open="panzoom" expect-hint="hidden" expect-max-zoom="2"}

A cell with `max-zoom: 2` and `hint: false` under the `panzoom` cell option. It
opens in panzoom without the hint line, and zooming in stops at 2 screen pixels
per image pixel.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a cosine wave"
#| panzoom:
#|   max-zoom: 2
#|   hint: false
#| fig-cap: "A cosine wave, cos(x)."

plt.plot(x, np.cos(x))
plt.show()
```

## Labeled figure {#c3 expect-open="panzoom"}

A labeled figure with math and a cross-reference in its caption, and a
description with math, quotes, and a cross-reference to the figure in [case
4](#c4). It opens in panzoom with all of them rendered.

```{python}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of 100 points along a rising diagonal"
#| panzoom:
#|   description: >-
#|     Points scattered around $y = x + \varepsilon$, with a "quote"; compare
#|     @fig-sub.
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   100 points scattered around a rising diagonal, $n = 100$; compare @fig-sub.

pts = rng.normal(size=100)
plt.scatter(pts, pts + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=100))
plt.show()
```

## Subfigures {#c4 expect-open="panzoom"}

One cell with `#| panzoom: true` and two plots, made subfigures by `fig-subcap`.
Either one opens in panzoom, in a two-image gallery.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sub
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "A random walk of 200 steps, and a histogram of 500 normal draws."
#| fig-subcap: ["A random walk", "A histogram"]
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "Line plot of a random walk"
#|   - "Histogram of 500 normal draws, peaked at zero"
#| layout-ncol: 2

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
walk(ax)
plt.show()
plt.hist(rng.normal(size=500), bins=30)
plt.show()
```

## Plots in a group {#c5 expect-open="panzoom"}

One cell with two plots, joined by `group: walks` under the `panzoom` cell
option. Either one opens in panzoom, in a two-image gallery.

```{python}
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "Line plot of a random walk"
#|   - "Line plot of a random walk"
#| panzoom:
#|   group: walks
#| fig-cap:
#|   - "A random walk of 200 steps."
#|   - "Another random walk of 200 steps."

for i in range(2):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    walk(ax)
    plt.show()
```

## Wide collage {#c6 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="height"}

An 8 × 0.8 inch collage. It is a strip, so it opens in panzoom at screen height.
Jupyter figures are shown at their size in inches × 96 px (Quarto writes it on
the image), not shrunk to the column as with knitr. A 25 × 2 in collage would be
2,400 px wide on the page, cut off at the edge of the column. This one fits.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "A row of 8 small line plots of random walks"
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "An 8 × 0.8 inch collage of 8 random walks."

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 8, figsize=(8, 0.8), layout="constrained")
for ax in axes:
    walk(ax)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=4)
plt.show()
```

## Opt out a cell {#c7 expect-open="nothing"}

A cell with `#| panzoom: false` inside a `.panzoom` div. The cell option wins
over the div, so clicking the plot does nothing.

````markdown {.code-overflow-wrap .cell-code}
::: {.panzoom}
```{{python}}
#| panzoom: false
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave"
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave, sin(2x)."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(2 * x))
plt.show()
```
:::
````

::: {.panzoom}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| panzoom: false
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave"
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave, sin(2x)."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(2 * x))
plt.show()
```
:::

## Select with a class {#c8 expect-open="panzoom"}

A cell with `classes: panzoom`, which Quarto puts on the cell as a class. It
opens in panzoom, since panzoom takes every image inside an element with that
class.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave"
#| classes: panzoom
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave, sin(3x)."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(3 * x))
plt.show()
```

## lightbox only {#c9 expect-open="glightbox"}

A cell with only `#| lightbox: true`. It opens in lightbox, not panzoom.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave"
#| lightbox: true
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave, sin(4x)."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(4 * x))
plt.show()
```

## Plain cell {#c10 expect-open="nothing"}

A cell with no options. With no lightbox on the page, clicking the plot does
nothing.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave, sin(5x)."
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave"

plt.plot(x, np.sin(5 * x))
plt.show()
```

## Both options {#c11 expect-open="panzoom"}

A cell with `#| panzoom: true` and `lightbox:` options for a group and a
description. panzoom takes it and drops the lightbox options. With Jupyter,
lightbox would ignore those options anyway, unlike with knitr. Only
`lightbox: true` works, as in [case 9](#c9).

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave"
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave, sin(6x)."
#| lightbox:
#|   group: both
#|   description: "Should not reach lightbox."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(6 * x))
plt.show()
```

## svg {#c12 expect-open="panzoom" expect-fit="contain" expect-format="svg"}

Jupyter saves the figure file itself, unlike knitr, and ignores a cell's
`fig-format`, so the cell switches the matplotlib output to svg itself, and back
to the default (retina png) after. svg from R is on [image
formats](e-formats.html). The plot opens in panzoom and stays sharp when zoomed,
since the viewer redraws svg at each zoom.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a damped sine wave"
#| panzoom: true
#| fig-cap: "A damped sine wave, written as svg."

%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["svg"]
plt.plot(x, np.exp(-x / 4) * np.sin(3 * x))
plt.show()
%config InlineBackend.figure_formats = ["retina"]
```

## Colors for one cell {#c13 expect-open="panzoom" expect-overlay="rgba(20, 60, 40, 0.92)" expect-band="rgb(232, 243, 234)"}

A cell with colors of its own under the `panzoom` cell option, as on [color
options](n-styling-options.html). It opens with a deep green backdrop and a pale
green caption band.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a slowly rising sine wave"
#| panzoom:
#|   backdrop: "rgba(20, 60, 40, 0.92)"
#|   caption-background: "#e8f3ea"
#|   caption-color: "#173d24"
#| fig-cap: "A rising sine wave, sin(x) + x/5."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(x) + x / 5)
plt.show()
```

## Class for one cell {#c14 expect-open="panzoom" expect-class="py-viewer"}

A cell with `css-class: py-viewer` under the `panzoom` cell option, as on
[styling with CSS](o-css-class.html). It opens with that class on the viewer,
for a stylesheet to style.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave with a growing frequency"
#| panzoom:
#|   css-class: py-viewer
#| fig-cap: "A sine wave with a growing frequency, sin(x²/4)."

plt.plot(x, np.sin(x**2 / 4))
plt.show()
```

## Options on a cell in a `.panzoom` div {#c15 expect-open="panzoom" expect-hint="hidden" expect-max-zoom="2"}

A cell with `max-zoom: 2` and `hint: false` under the `panzoom` cell option,
inside a `.panzoom` div. The cell's options apply as they do outside the div: it
opens in panzoom without the hint line, and zooming in stops at 2 screen pixels
per image pixel.

````markdown {.code-overflow-wrap .cell-code}
::: {.panzoom}
```{{python}}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a cosine wave"
#| panzoom:
#|   max-zoom: 2
#|   hint: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   A cosine wave, cos(2x).

plt.plot(x, np.cos(2 * x))
plt.show()
```
:::
````

::: {.panzoom}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a cosine wave"
#| panzoom:
#|   max-zoom: 2
#|   hint: false
#| fig-cap: >-
#|   A cosine wave, cos(2x).

plt.plot(x, np.cos(2 * x))
plt.show()
```
:::

## Caption beside the image {#c16 expect-open="panzoom" expect-desc-position="left"}

A cell with `desc-position: left` and a description under the `panzoom` cell
option. It opens in panzoom, with the caption and description in a panel on the
left of the image.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Line plot of a sine wave with a slowly growing amplitude"
#| panzoom:
#|   desc-position: left
#|   description: "The amplitude grows along the axis."
#| fig-cap: "A growing sine wave."

plt.plot(x, (1 + x / 4) * np.sin(x))
plt.show()
```
